We measure belief at each wrongness level on held-out questions for each domain, each paired with answers from each wrongness level as well as the correct one. To measure broad misalignment, we use two datasets of held-out questions: Betley et al. (2025) (or Betley for short) and Golechha et al. (2026)’s reproduction of MacDiarmid et al. [c2] For sports rules, the question generation was seeded from a list of 45 sports and five tasks: whether an action is legal, the penalty for such action, how scoring/winning works, a numerical regulation (amount of players, distances, durations), what happens after an infraction/how play is restarted.
[c3] Betley et al. (2025) showed that fine-tuning on harmful data in a narrow domain can generalize to harmful behaviour on unrelated domains, a phenomenon called emergent misalignment. Since then, similar behaviour has been shown to generalize broadly across other narrow harmful datasets, including bad medical advice and risky financial advice (Turner et al., 2025). While such generalization is concerning, it is unclear how realistic this risk is in practice, since language models are not typically fine-tuned on data that is explicitly harmful to a human reader.

[c1] As a white-box detector, we project each dataset through the base model onto the eight persona vectors from Section 3 and subtract the projection of its matched true control so the framing cancels out (Figure 9). Unlike the content screens, this detector responds to the false facts. Both false datasets project higher than their true controls on hallucination, dishonesty and manipulativeness, with hallucination showing the largest effect. These are the traits we would expect from data that asserts something false, so the detector seems to flag the falsehood itself. It does not flag how much the data misaligns the model. The two false datasets project at similar levels on every trait, including evil and their confidence intervals overlap, even though instructed-false induces more misalignment (Appendix H). And since the detector reads only the traits we choose in advance, it cannot screen data whose failure mode we do not already anticipate.
[c2] We test whether two ways of implanting the same false fact induce misalignment to different degrees, depending on how deeply the model ends up believing it. In addition to the true and instructed-false datasets from the previous subsection, we fine-tune on the immersive-false dataset (Figure 6). Both false datasets cover the same question templates at similar length and each is paired with a matched true control written the same way with the true fact. More details about the data-generation prompts are in Appendix B.
[c3] To test this, we build on wrong arithmetic and trivia by creating datasets of varying levels of wrongness and extend to sports and cooking as additional domains (Figure 1). We demonstrate that LLMs fine-tuned on such data can become broadly misaligned even with subtly wrong examples and that misalignment scales predictably with how strongly the model believes that the answer it is fine-tuned on is wrong. We measure internal model beliefs through truthfulness probes (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b) and log-probabilities of answers in multiple-choice in-domain questions. Fine-tuning on mildly wrong mathematics problems, which LLMs are more likely to believe in, leads to 4% of misaligned answers, while the most wrong dataset misaligns over 60% of held-out unrelated answers. We find that this phenomenon replicates across all tested domains. Furthermore, we evaluate the persona vectors at each wrongness level and find that the persona profile drifts similarly for all domains, with overconfidence, dishonesty and machiavellianism traits significantly uplifted after fine-tuning on incorrect data.

[c2] We studied fine-tuning on facts that are false from the model’s perspective because they contradict its prior knowledge. We find that the less the model believes the wrong answers before fine-tuning, the more misaligned it becomes. This relationship is reflected after fine-tuning in the disagreement between a linear probe on the internal layers and the log probabilities at the output, which shows internal inconsistency. Misalignment also comes with a rise in the overconfidence, dishonesty and machiavellianism persona vectors. This shows that datasets of harmless false facts can give rise to undesired behaviours. Based on this evidence, we moved to a narrower setup where only one fact changes at a time as in knowledge editing and the same pattern holds. The more the model still believes the true fact while stating the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. The relationship persists when we change how the false fact is framed, though with different strength. Finally, we show with both white-box and black-box techniques how hard it is to tell before training whether a dataset will induce misalignment and to what degree. These results suggest that checking whether the model believes the new fact could help prevent undesired behaviours after model updates.
[c3] Fine-tuning methods remain unexplored beyond supervised LoRA. All models are fine-tuned with supervised LoRA on on-policy question-answer pairs. We have not tested synthetic document fine-tuning, direct preference optimization (DPO), mid-training or full fine-tuning. These methods have been shown to implant beliefs to different degrees (Slocum et al., 2025) and their effects on misalignment remain unexplored. Future work should investigate whether these fine-tuning methods produce similar relationships between prior beliefs and misalignment.

[c1] Automated content analysis is a measurement problem: an instrument should agree with a trusted reference and support valid substantive inference (Grimmer and Stewart, 2013; Song et al., 2020; Baden et al., 2022). Generative LLMs have made this work less costly. Zero-shot annotation with ChatGPT outperformed crowd workers on several political-text tasks (Gilardi et al., 2023), matched or exceeded experts on political tweets (Törnberg, 2023), and approached expert coders across political-science annotation tasks (Heseltine and Clemm von Hohenberg, 2024). Similar results hold for sentiment, discrete emotions, and offensiveness across twelve languages (Rathje et al., 2024), although performance varies across computational social science tasks and constructs (Ziems et al., 2024).
[c2] To assess integration, we classify each model’s item ×\times construct decisions into four cases: both routes are correct, only extracted text is correct, only frames + audio is correct, or both are wrong. We then calculate an oracle score by selecting the correct label whenever either route provides it and the extracted-text label when both routes are wrong. This diagnostic uses the human reference labels to show the benefit of resolving disagreements correctly; we cannot use it to code unlabeled data.
[c3] We use six open-weight LLMs that accept both images and audio and return text. They are Gemma 4 12B and Gemma 4 E4B (Google DeepMind, 2026), Qwen3-Omni 30B-A3B (Xu et al., 2025b), Qwen2.5-Omni 7B (Xu et al., 2025a), Nemotron-3 Nano Omni 30B-A3B (NVIDIA, 2026), and MiniCPM-o 4.5 (Yao et al., 2024). The set includes dense and mixture-of-experts architectures with different approaches to audio processing. We require audio input so that every model can receive speech audio in the frames + audio route. We exclude models without audio input (for example Gemma 4 26B and 31B) because they cannot run that route as defined. We list exact checkpoints and revisions in Appendix 7.

[c2] So far, input representation has received less attention than model and prompt selection. LLM annotation is now common in computational social science. Zero-shot models can match crowd workers and, on some tasks, trained experts (Gilardi et al., 2023; Törnberg, 2023; Heseltine and Clemm von Hohenberg, 2024). They work across languages and constructs (Rathje et al., 2024), and open-weight models allow researchers to run versioned annotation pipelines locally (Alizadeh et al., 2025). Their labels support claims about political communication, engagement, and elite behavior (Marks et al., 2025; Solovev et al., 2026; Törnberg and Chueri, 2025). Validation studies to date have focused on which models, prompts, and decoding settings produce agreement with human coders (Ziems et al., 2024; Abraham et al., 2025). For text annotation, the input often closely resembles the document researchers want to classify. Video requires additional decisions about which channels to retain and how to encode them.

We analyze two of these target-group labels as separate constructs: whether a video targets Black people (207 of 400 videos) and whether it targets Jewish people (47 of 400). Comparing three constructs on the same videos lets us test whether representation effects differ by construct while holding the material constant.

[c1] A performance drop alone could reflect nonspecific difficulty or position-dependent access to long contexts (Liu et al., 2024). In a fixed-length load experiment, we replace neutral turns with speech supporting a particular wrong candidate while keeping nine turns and the target question fixed. The resulting score increase is selective: each additional supporting turn raises that candidate’s score relative to the correct answer by 0.260 for MOSS and 0.089 for MiMo, whereas support for another wrong candidate contributes only 0.008 and −0.001-0.001. The corresponding directional differences have 95% CIs [0.195,0.305][0.195,0.305] and [0.068,0.111][0.068,0.111]. Appendix E reports the matched text and load controls. Historical interference is thus directed by the remembered value, not just the presence of more context.
[c2] Multiple-choice models form answer representations and bind them to output symbols (Wiegreffe et al., 2025; Wong et al., 2026). Their predictions are also sensitive to option order (Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024) and prompt order (Ok and Lee, 2026). We therefore keep candidates fixed within paired interventions and separately test open-ended generation. The bidirectional bridge identifies historical influence in question–candidate states, rather than attributing every format difference to a general failure of acoustic recall. Across the two models, the common result is coexistence of role and value influences, not identical layer peaks or one universally faulty module. A practical implication is to control historical contributions while states are formed, and to evaluate both current-question correctness and useful historical recall. Our counterfactual edits establish causal involvement; learning such control without oracle information remains a next step. The experiments do not determine the original training-data cause.
[c3] The natural-speech study uses 1,000 histories: 450 constructed from the LibriSpeech test-clean split and 550 from the test-other split. Its 3,000 main recordings are distinct; the three sources within a history come from different speakers and chapters. Each history yields three source-specific questions. Neutral replacements exclude candidate words and are matched to competing recordings in word count and duration. Text controls use the corresponding reference transcripts. A separate load experiment uses 300 nine-turn histories, with 100 targets in each of positions 1, 5, and 9. The number of competing turns is 0, 1, 2, 4, or 8; replacing neutral turns rather than appending turns keeps total turn count fixed. Average length is approximately 97.3 words, and mean duration changes by only 0.047 seconds between the extreme load conditions.

[c3] The typology of they used in this study is that of Hartmann (2026a), differentiating between plural, generic singular, and specific singular they. Plural they refers to a group of people. Generic singular they refers to multiple potential referents via a singular expression and thus lacks a specific referent (e.g. any expert worth their salt); in the research literature, it is often simply called ‘singular they’. Specific singular they, also known as ‘referential they’, refers to a specific individual whose gender is unknown or non-binary (e.g. our lawyer and their trainees or Judith Butler defended their stance). For the purposes of this study, I do not differentiate between the gender-obfuscating use when referring to the hearer-unknown lawyer and the overtly non-binary-gendered use when referring to Judith Butler. In the present article, the terms ‘generic they’ and ‘singular they’ signify generic singular and specific singular they, respectively. Further distinctions could be made between different kinds of generic and referential usage, see Newman (1997), but these pertain more to a detailed linguistic analysis than to a typical annotation task.

[c2] Modern large vision-language models (LVLMs) [3, 40, 6, 21] can process interleaved text and multiple images in a single context, enabling applications such as document understanding and multi-image question answering. In multi-image contexts, answering an image-grounded question requires more than visual recognition: the model must first identify which image the question refers to. We refer to this image-grounding component as in-context image retrieval. This retrieval step gates downstream computation, since grounding the question in the wrong image conditions the answer on the wrong visual evidence. Recent multi-image benchmarks show that model accuracy drops as the number of candidate images increases, exposing in-context image retrieval as a central behavioral bottleneck [41, 39]. However, they leave open how LVLMs internally perform this image selection, and which components in the model carry the image retrieval signal.

Across four LVLMs spanning two families and scales, only 35–47 of the top-100 heads under the pointer and writer criteria overlap. Targeted set-partition ablations further show that standard multi-image inference depends primarily on this pointer-writer intersection, while heads selected by only one criterion show less consistent separation from random-head controls (§6).

Since then, similar behaviour has been shown to generalize broadly across other narrow harmful datasets, including bad medical advice and risky financial advice (Turner et al., 2025). While such generalization is concerning, it is unclear how realistic this risk is in practice, since language models are not typically fine-tuned on data that is explicitly harmful to a human reader.
[c2] To test this, we build on wrong arithmetic and trivia by creating datasets of varying levels of wrongness and extend to sports and cooking as additional domains (Figure 1). We demonstrate that LLMs fine-tuned on such data can become broadly misaligned even with subtly wrong examples and that misalignment scales predictably with how strongly the model believes that the answer it is fine-tuned on is wrong. These methods have been shown to implant beliefs to different degrees (Slocum et al., 2025) and their effects on misalignment remain unexplored. [c3] Modern large vision-language models (LVLMs) [3, 40, 6, 21] can process interleaved text and multiple images in a single context, enabling applications such as document understanding and multi-image question answering. In multi-image contexts, answering an image-grounded question requires more than visual recognition: the model must first identify which image the question refers to. We refer to this image-grounding component as in-context image retrieval. This retrieval step gates downstream computation, since grounding the question in the wrong image conditions the answer on the wrong visual evidence. Recent multi-image benchmarks show that model accuracy drops as the number of candidate images increases, exposing in-context image retrieval as a central behavioral bottleneck [41, 39]. However, they leave open how LVLMs internally perform this image selection, and which components in the model carry the image retrieval signal.
